title: Raga Kedara

lines: DISHES, A DOOR, THE DAY REPLAYING.
cards: Evening has its own sound. Dishes clinking. A door closing down the hall.
The day's conversations still replaying: who praised you, who didn't, what someone said that stung.
Right about then, as the house goes quiet, tradition sets a raga down gently: Kedara, a short section of the Guru Granth Sahib this path calls tender, for the evening.
And inside it is a hymn that speaks straight to those replaying conversations.

teach.h: GURUS FIRST, THEN KABIR AND RAVIDAS.
teach.b: Kedara holds hymns of Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan, and after them the voices of Bhagats, Kabir and Ravidas.
Today, Kabir, in plain English, not word for word: set aside both praise and slander; give up pride and self-conceit.
The one who looks on iron and gold alike, Kabir says, is an image of God. Here's how evening can go. The compliments get replayed and polished.
The criticism gets replayed and argued with. Both keep the mind awake. Kabir asks for something quieter: let go of both.
Not just the insult. The praise too. That's the tender part, and the hard part; setting down a compliment can feel like losing something.
One way to read Kabir: praise and blame both tie a person to other people's opinions, and a mind can't rest while it's tied. Iron and gold alike isn't a rule against nice things.
It's a picture of a mind that doesn't jump when the world calls it gold, and doesn't sink when the world calls it iron. Evening is a good place for that hymn.

teach.h: DON'T CARRY THE VERDICTS TO BED.
teach.b: The day's verdicts are in, and this is when you can decide not to carry them to bed. Tomorrow, another Bhagat in this raga, at dusk.

how: Shabads from the Kedara section, including the Bhagats' hymns by Kabir and Ravidas, are sung in Raga Kedara in kirtan, and tradition associates the raga with the evening.

o: a short, tender raga of the evening
a festive raga sung only at weddings
a stern raga sung at the start of the day

games.q: what's inside the raga — tap the pairs.

s: Kabir only asks you to let go of insults
he asks for both: set aside praise and slander alike.
Kedara holds hymns by Bhagats as well as Gurus
Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan, then Kabir and Ravidas.
'iron and gold alike' is a rule against owning nice things
it pictures a mind that doesn't jump at praise or sink at blame.

games.q: it's evening. someone praised you today, and someone else criticized you. what does Kabir's Kedara hymn ask?
o: keep the praise, drop the criticism.
games.why: Kabir: set aside both praise and slander, and look on iron and gold alike. the praise goes too.

practice: Bring to mind one piece of praise from this week and one piece of criticism, and if it helps, picture one in each hand, gold and iron, noticing which feels heavier.
Then, on an out-breath, set them both down beside you, like two bags at the end of a long walk. If you pray, say Waheguru as you set them down; if you don't, simply let your hands rest open.

wordCard.voice: Raga Kedara. A short, tender evening raga where Kabir sings: set aside praise and slander, and look on iron and gold alike. Today's word.

orig.note: kedara: the raga named at the head of this short evening section of the Guru Granth Sahib.

carryVoice: Your line: tender evening. The day's verdicts don't have to come to bed with you. See you tomorrow.
